title: I used AI to turn everyday objects into chemistry cards, then made them collide with Three.js
author: BluebirdSalty8162
selftext:
I wanted to make a small chemistry game that felt more like discovering reactions than memorizing a periodic table.The basic idea is simple: pick two element cards, throw them into an arena, and see what happens.

The first difficult part was keeping the cards visually consistent.

Instead of putting a large element symbol on every card, I wanted each one to be associated with a familiar object or scene from everyday life. The hope was that players could remember the element through an image, rather than another block of text. I built the project in HappySeeds. It first generated several possible card directions for me. I picked a hand-drawn comic style, then used that as the reference for generating the rest of the element cards as one set.That saved a lot of time, but I still had to make decisions about composition, visual associations, readability, and whether the cards actually looked like they belonged in the same game.

The second problem was the collision itself.

My first version only moved two static cards toward each other. Technically it worked, but it felt more like a UI transition than a game. So I split the reactions into several visual families, including explosions, fire, flashes, smoke, crystals, and no reaction. I also added different product types, such as liquids, gases, powders, metals, acids, and crystals.Three.js effects for these reactions are generated. The cards remain standard React elements, with a separate Three.js layer managing particles, lighting, shockwaves, smoke, and crystal growth.

That small change made the whole thing feel much more alive.The part I am still working through is where game logic and real chemistry disagree. Some combinations require specific conditions, while others should not react at all. I do not want to present made-up chemistry as educational fact just because it produces a better animation.

Right now I am considering two approaches:

1. Only show full effects for verified reactions, and let everything else bounce back with an explanation.
2. Keep a separate “battle mode” with simplified rules, while clearly separating it from the educational reaction mode.

Which approach would make more sense to you?

comments.author: tangerine-94
comments.body: this idea’s way better than the periodic table，what model did you use to generate these cards?

replies.author: BluebirdSalty8162
replies.body: The cards were generated using the built-in image generation model in HappySeeds.

comments.author: Tok-A-Mak
comments.body: Looks fun. But may need some more reactions. I just failed combining Li+Cl into Lithiumchloride and rusting up Iron with Oxygen also didn't work as I would have expected.

replies.author: BluebirdSalty8162
replies.body: Thanks for the feedback. I plan to generate all elements of the periodic table next and correct their corresponding chemical reaction data. This work does require a solid grasp of chemistry knowledge.

comments.author: No-Spring1312
comments.body: Verified reaction mode plus a separate battle mode feels like the cleanest split, otherwise education gets messy fast.

replies.author: BluebirdSalty8162
replies.body: I hope players can pick up relevant chemistry knowledge naturally while playing.
